title: Welby Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Welby-area wells have a 32-foot median depth, but monitoring wells dominate the records. Compare yields, drilling costs and buyer risks.
h1: Welby well depths, costs and land-buying checks
intro_html:
A shallow well record near Welby does not necessarily tell you what a household water supply will require. Colorado DWR records within 5 miles include 10,456 permits, and monitoring accounts for 64% of the reported use mix. Domestic and household uses account for 14%.

The recorded median depth is 32 feet, but that figure needs context before you use it to price a project. For property in Welby or toward Sherrelwood, North Washington and Twin Lakes, start by separating nearby water-supply wells from monitoring installations.

sections.heading: Welby’s shallow records need a closer look
sections.html:
Among the 6,079 records reporting depth, the median is 32 feet and the middle half runs from 20 to 49 feet. That is a shallow recorded range, not a dependable target for a new domestic well. Monitoring wells dominate the local permit inventory and may be completed for a different purpose than supplying a home.

Depths under 100 feet account for 89% of the reported mix, yet the deepest record reaches 1,751 feet. Permits include Alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium aquifer labels, while the drilling cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. A useful bid needs the intended aquifer, permitted use and comparable supply-well logs—not just the area median.

sections.heading: Reported yields look strong, but the sample is small
sections.html:
Only 266 records report a pump yield. Within that sample, the median is 34.0 gpm and the middle half spans 15.0–130.0 gpm. Those results suggest productive wells are present around Welby, but they do not establish what an untested parcel will produce.

The reported yield mix has 76% at 15+ gpm, 2% at 1–5 gpm and 0% under 1 gpm. That last figure is not proof that low-yield or unsuccessful wells are absent. Before buying, obtain the actual well’s pumping-test report and check sustained production and recovery. Reported pump capacity also does not establish the amount or uses legally allowed under its DWR permit.

sections.heading: Water is shallow in the measurements—not steadily dropping
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to standing water in a resting well, not the well’s total drilled depth. The 282 Welby-area records with measurements have a median of 10 feet below ground, with the middle half between 7 and 23 feet.

The decade medians are 24 feet in the 1960s, 23 feet in the 2000s, 10 feet in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s. These figures do not show a progressively dropping water table; the later medians are shallower. They also are not repeat measurements from a fixed set of wells. For excavation, septic design or basement planning, investigate seasonal groundwater on the parcel rather than treating the regional median as a design elevation.

sections.heading: Welby’s permit activity includes substantial monitoring work
sections.html:
The inventory lists 5,292 wells as constructed out of 10,456 permit records. Permits are not interchangeable with completed, operating household wells. Recorded issuance includes 1,637 permits in the 1990s, 1,659 in the 2000s and 2,610 in the 2010s. The 2020s have 996, with the newest permit dated 2025; that is not a complete-decade comparison.

The most frequent driller-field entry is “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” at 3,289 records. Treat that as a recorded label, not a contractor recommendation. Named entries include Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.) with 202 and Ground Exploration Llc (Bender, Joseph T.) with 102. Historical record counts do not establish current availability or suitability for a domestic project.

sections.heading: Budget beyond the drilled hole in Welby
sections.html:
The supplied cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock at $50–$70 per foot. Applied to the recorded 32-foot median, it puts the drilled hole at about $1,600–$2,200 and a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical at about $7,600–$14,200.

Use that as a model, not a parcel quote. The depth statistics include substantial monitoring activity, so the median may not represent the supply well your home needs. Ask bidders to state the target depth and aquifer, casing and grout scope, pump equipment, access requirements and exclusions. A deeper required completion or difficult equipment access can change the project substantially, even when nearby mapped wells appear shallow.

sections.heading: Cleanup records and shallow groundwater deserve attention
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles of Welby, the mapped environmental inventory includes 686 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 175 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. These are screening records across a broad area—not evidence that every nearby well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location also does not, by itself, establish a detection in your water.

Check each relevant site’s status, groundwater findings and relationship to the parcel. Have a qualified laboratory test the actual supply, with analytes selected for local conditions and site history. A depth log or strong yield cannot establish drinking-water safety. For construction, coordinate well placement, septic suitability, drainage and excavation planning before fixing the house location; shallow groundwater can constrain the layout.

sections.heading: Before closing on land near Welby
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s water-service options and DWR permit status. Do not assume an existing monitoring well can supply a residence or that a household-use permit allows irrigation. New withdrawals may face water-rights restrictions, and an augmentation plan may be needed where applicable.

Compare nearby records toward North Washington, Derby or Federal Heights, but match intended use and aquifer before comparing depths. Request the permit, completion log, pumping test, water-quality results and any abandonment records. Make the purchase decision depend on a legal, workable supply—not a nearby map marker. For an undeveloped lot, settle rig access, well and septic placement, utility routing and the building footprint together before committing to the site plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Welby, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Welby, recorded well depths have a median of 32 feet, with the middle half between 20 and 49 feet. However, monitoring accounts for 64% of the use mix. A new household well may need a different completion depth, so compare nearby supply wells in the intended aquifer before relying on that median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Welby?
faq.a: The supplied model estimates $50–$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the recorded 32-foot median, that means about $1,600–$2,200 for the hole or $7,600–$14,200 finished with pump, tank, trenching and electrical. Because monitoring wells dominate the records, get a parcel-specific depth and construction proposal before using those figures as your budget.

faq.q: How much water do wells in Welby produce?
faq.a: The 266 records reporting pump yield have a median of 34.0 gpm, with the middle half between 15.0 and 130.0 gpm. That is a limited sample of the local inventory, not a guarantee for your property. Review a sustained pumping test and recovery results, and verify that the permit allows your intended household and outdoor uses.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Welby?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. The nearby mapped inventory includes 686 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 175 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but those counts do not prove contamination at a particular well. Review relevant cleanup records and arrange laboratory testing of the actual water supply before relying on it for drinking.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Welby?
faq.a: The supplied measurements do not show a steadily dropping water table. Median depth to water was 24 feet in the 1960s and 9 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later median is shallower. However, these decade groups are not repeated measurements from the same wells. They cannot establish the long-term groundwater trend at an individual parcel.
